title: McGee v. International Life Insurance Co. (1957)
summary: A single insurance relationship had a sufficient California connection when the insurer solicited the agreement there and the suit arose from that agreement.
notes:
Hanson immediately qualifies an expansive reading: a plaintiff’s unilateral relocation is not equivalent to an insurer’s own solicitation into the forum. McGee does not make every contract with a resident sufficient.

Franklin bought the policy in 1944 from Empire Mutual, an Arizona company; International Life, a Texas corporation, assumed its obligations in 1948 and Franklin mailed premiums from California until his death in 1950. McGee, his mother and beneficiary, sued under California's statute permitting service on out-of-state insurers.

sections.Parties: McGee, the beneficiary of Franklin’s life insurance, sued International Life, a Texas insurer that had assumed the original insurer’s obligations.
sections.Material Facts: Franklin lived in California. After taking over the policy, International Life mailed him a reinsurance certificate offering to insure him on the existing terms. Franklin accepted and sent premiums from California. On his death, the insurer refused payment, contending that he had committed suicide. The company’s lack of other substantial California business did not remove the deliberate connection created by this particular insurance relationship.
sections.Procedural History: McGee obtained a California judgment after using the state’s procedure for serving the out-of-state insurer. The Texas courts refused to enforce that judgment on jurisdictional grounds. The Supreme Court reversed that refusal.
sections.Issue: Could California exercise jurisdiction over the insurer on this policy claim even though the company’s forum contact was essentially the single contract?
sections.Holding: Yes. The contract had a substantial connection with California, and the claim arose from that contract.
sections.Reasoning: The insurer’s own mailing sought an ongoing relationship with a California insured. Acceptance, premium payments, and the insured risk connected the claim to that state. California also had an interest in giving residents effective redress against insurers, while requiring beneficiaries to sue far away could make modest claims impractical. Those features supported a fair forum for this dispute despite the small number of transactions. The case’s significance is qualitative: a deliberate, suit-related contact can matter more than a large count of unrelated contacts.

learning.why: A single insurance relationship had a sufficient California connection when the insurer solicited the agreement there and the suit arose from that agreement.

topics.purposeful-availment: The insurer deliberately sent the certificate into California to continue the insurance relationship.
topics.relatedness: The beneficiary’s claim arose from the very insurance contract connected to California.
topics.fairness: California’s interest and the practical difficulty of small claims against distant insurers supported jurisdiction.
topics.cp-contractual-contacts: The single insurance contract solicited by mail into California is the paradigm of a contract as a forum contact.
topics.specific-jurisdiction: Jurisdiction rested on a single contact from which the claim arose, the essence of specific jurisdiction.
topics.cp-long-arm: California's Unauthorized Insurers Process Act supplied the statutory authorization for service on the Texas insurer.
